# looop 0.43.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/looop/0.43.1

# looop

A tiny, portable, autonomous control loop for agent-driven work. One self-contained binary — no database, no server, no helper files.

## The idea

**looop is the brain, not a task runner.** It watches the things you care about
(GitHub, Linear, Grafana, …) and runs a fleet of worker agents. Each beat it
senses the world and, if something changed, decides the *single* most important
move and executes it — including spawning workers. The judgment lives *inside*
looop (a small, gated LLM call per beat).

An autonomous loop is easy. The hard part — and the whole point of looop's
design — is **where and how a human enters the loop.** Too much human and it
isn't autonomous; too little and it's reckless. looop's answer is to pull you in
at exactly two kinds of moments, and nowhere else.

## How the human stays in the loop

There are two distinct ways you touch the loop — and that split *is* the design.

**Steer — async, you initiate.** You are a peer, not a driver. You shape *what*
looop pursues by editing goals and the PLAYBOOK; it observes them next beat. This
never blocks the loop — you set direction and walk away.

**Answer — sync, the loop initiates.** looop reaches back for *you* only when it
genuinely must: a worker hits a decision only a human can make, or an
irreversible action — merge, deploy, delete — needs an explicit yes. It blocks
and waits for your call.

The key move: **the intervention point is decoupled from any UI.** Asks and
answers are a durable file mailbox reached through one backend-agnostic contract
(`looop _ …`), so the loop never blocks on a particular terminal, tmux, or stdin
— it just needs an answer *eventually*, from whatever channel reaches you:

- a **bare terminal**— you typing the verbs yourself (the thinnest client);
- an **agent concierge**— a`claude`/`codex`/`opencode`/`pi`session that relays asks in plain language and answers on your behalf;
- a **notify script**— a loop that pushes asks to Slack/SMS and relays your reply.

A client is an *interface*, never a decision-maker. looop decides; the client
just carries the question to you and your answer back.

Two properties make all this dependable:

- **Level-triggered.**All state is plain files, so the loop re-senses every beat and a crashed pulse just re-reads its files on restart. A pending ask survives restarts — no queues, no lost work.
- **One move per beat.**Each beat does at most one thing; a daily budget caps spend. Behavior stays legible and cheap — an unchanged world costs no LLM call.

## One beat: sense → decide → act

- **SENSE**— run every- `sensors/*.sh`, refreshing- `snapshots/`. World unchanged since last beat → stop here, no LLM call.
- **DECIDE**— on change, hand the PLAYBOOK + goals + readings + pending asks to the LLM, which returns- **one**typed move.
- **ACT**— execute it: write a goal/sensor/PLAYBOOK, run one reversible command, or spawn a worker. Irreversible moves are gated — they wait for your- `answer`(see above), and so does any worker that hits a human-only decision.

## Three layers

| Layer | What it is |
|---|---|
| core | the autonomous pulse + the durable state behind it. Decides and acts. |
| contract | the `looop _ …`verbs — the one stable, backend-agnostic surface to read and steer core. |
| client | anything that drives the contract for a human (terminal / concierge / notify). An interface, never a decision-maker. |

State is plain files in the data dir, reached *through* the contract — not a
public interface:

| File / dir | Role |
|---|---|
| `PLAYBOOK.md` | your judgment, priorities, guardrails |
| `goals/*.md` | desired state — one declarative spec per thing you push |
| `sensors/*.sh` | observers — each prints one JSON object |
| `journal.md` | action log — one line per move |
| `asks/``answers/` | the worker ↔ human mailbox |

## Install

```
 |
# or
```
**Only hard dependency:** an LLM runner. `claude` is the default; `codex`,
`opencode`, and `pi` also work — pick one with `looop init`. (Workers that touch
code isolate their own sandbox via `git worktree` — a worker convention, not a
looop dependency.)

## Usage

The pulse refuses to start until `looop init` writes the runner wiring, so the
agent CLI driving every tick and worker is always an explicit choice. Read and
steer core with the `looop _ …` verbs (`_ state`, `_ wait`, `_ answer`,
`_ goal write`), by hand or through a client.

### First run

looop runs headless, so it can't interview you. A fresh data dir is seeded with a
starter PLAYBOOK, a `setup` goal, and a real pending `setup` ask so a client
waiting on asks wakes immediately.

Start with `looop up` then `looop client`: the TUI keeps the pending ask list on
screen and lets you answer by hand — no extra tooling, just looop. Answer the
starter `setup` ask, edit your goals/PLAYBOOK with the `looop _ …` verbs, archive
the `setup` goal, and looop runs from there.

**Even easier: an agent concierge.** Point a `claude`/`codex`/`opencode`/`pi`
session at looop and talk to it in plain language — it relays asks with
recommendations, drives the write verbs for you, and interviews you to shape your
goals, sensors, and PLAYBOOK:

```
# "be my looop concierge: run `looop up`, relay the setup goal, and interview
#  me to write my goals, sensors, and PLAYBOOK."
```
See `looop help` for the full command reference and design manual.

## Configuration

The config (`$LOOOP_CONFIG`, default `~/.config/looop/config.json`) is just **two
shell commands**. `looop init` lets you pick `claude`, `codex`, `opencode`, `pi`,
or `custom`; after that looop treats the result as plain runner wiring:

| Key | Role |
|---|---|
| `tick_command` | run ONE disposable decision. The prompt is passed via the `{{prompt_file}}`placeholder (substituted with the prompt file path — read it with`$(cat {{prompt_file}})`or`@{{prompt_file}}`). If you omit the placeholder the prompt is piped in onstdininstead. Must run unattended (no permission prompts — the detached pulse can't answer them) and emit a structured event stream looop can render. |
| `worker_command` | launch a worker agent. Same `{{prompt_file}}`placeholder, substituted with the worker's prompt file path. (A worker can't use the stdin fallback — stdin is its live attach TTY.) It may also carry`{{model}}`and`{{thinking}}`placeholders for per-worker model selection (see below). |

**Per-worker model selection.** The `worker_command` may include `{{model}}` and `{{thinking}}` placeholders. When a worker starts they are substituted with, in precedence order: the `looop _ worker start --model M --thinking L` flags, then the optional top-level `worker_model` / `worker_thinking` config keys, then the empty string. A template that omits a placeholder is left untouched, so configs and flag-less starts behave exactly as before; passing `--model` against a template with no `{{model}}` placeholder logs a warning and is ignored. Example wiring:

```
```

```

```
**opencode** (best-effort — verify against your installed version)

resolve to the latest of each; pin a specific version (e.g.
`--model claude-opus-4-1`) if you need reproducibility.

# relative-path 2.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/relative-path/2.0.1

# relative-path

Portable relative UTF-8 paths for Rust.

This crate provides a module analogous to [ std::path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/index.html), with the following
characteristics:

- The path separator is set to a fixed character (`/`), regardless of platform.
- Relative paths cannot represent a path in the filesystem without first
specifying *what they are relative to*using functions such as`to_path``to_logical_path`
- Relative paths are always guaranteed to be valid UTF-8 strings.

On top of this we support many operations that guarantee the same behavior across platforms.

For more utilities to manipulate relative paths, see the
[ relative-path-utils crate](https://docs.rs/relative-path-utils).

## Usage

Add `relative-path` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
 = "2.0.1"
```
Start using relative paths:

```
use ;
use RelativePath;
```
## Serde Support

This library includes serde support that can be enabled with the `serde`
feature.

## Why is `std::path` a portability hazard?

Path representations differ across platforms.

- Windows permits using drive volumes (multiple roots) as a prefix (e.g.
`"c:\"`) and backslash (`\`) as a separator.
- Unix references absolute paths from a single root and uses forward slash
(`/`) as a separator.

If we use `PathBuf`, Storing paths in a manifest would allow our application
to build and run on one platform but potentially not others.

Consider the following data model and corresponding toml for a manifest:

```
use PathBuf;
use ;
```
```
 = "C:\\Users\\udoprog\\repo\\data\\source"
```
This will run for you (assuming `source` exists). So you go ahead and check
the manifest into git. The next day your Linux colleague calls you and
wonders what they have ever done to wrong you?

So what went wrong? Well two things. You forgot to make the `source`
relative, so anyone at the company which has a different username than you
won't be able to use it. So you go ahead and fix that:

```
 = "data\\source"
```
But there is still one problem! A backslash (`\`) is only a legal path
separator on Windows. Luckily you learn that forward slashes are supported
both on Windows *and* Linux. So you opt for:

```
 = "data/source"
```
Things are working now. So all is well... Right? Sure, but we can do better.

This crate provides types that work with *portable relative paths* (hence
the name). So by using [ RelativePath](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html) we can systematically help avoid
portability issues like the one above. Avoiding issues at the source is
preferably over spending 5 minutes of onboarding time on a theoretical
problem, hoping that your new hires will remember what to do if they ever
encounter it.

Using [ RelativePathBuf](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePathBuf.html) we can fix our data model like this:

```
use RelativePathBuf;
use ;
```
And where it's used:

```
use fs;
use current_dir;
let manifest: Manifest = todo!;
let root = current_dir?;
let source = manifest.source.to_path;
let content = read?;
```
## Overview

Conversion to a platform-specific [ Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html) happens through the

[and](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.to_path)

`to_path`[functions. Where you are required to specify the path that prefixes the relative path. This can come from a function such as](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.to_logical_path)

`to_logical_path`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/env/fn.current_dir.html)

`std::env::current_dir````
use current_dir;
use Path;
use RelativePath;
let root = current_dir?;
// to_path unconditionally concatenates a relative path with its base:
let relative_path = new;
let full_path = relative_path.to_path;
assert_eq!;
// to_logical_path tries to apply the logical operations that the relative
// path corresponds to:
let relative_path = new;
let full_path = relative_path.to_logical_path;
// Replicate the operation performed by `to_logical_path`.
let mut parent = root.clone;
parent.pop;
assert_eq!;
```
When two relative paths are compared to each other, their exact component makeup determines equality.

```
use RelativePath;
assert_ne!;
```
Using platform-specific path separators to construct relative paths is not supported.

Path separators from other platforms are simply treated as part of a component:

```
use RelativePath;
assert_ne!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
To see if two relative paths are equivalent you can use [ normalize](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.normalize):

```
use RelativePath;
assert_eq!;
```
## Additional portability notes

While relative paths avoid the most egregious portability issue, that absolute paths will work equally unwell on all platforms. We cannot avoid all. This section tries to document additional portability hazards that we are aware of.

[ RelativePath](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html), similarly to

[, makes no guarantees that its constituent components make up legal file names. While components are strictly separated by slashes, we can still store things in them which may not be used as legal paths on all platforms.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`- A `NUL`character is not permitted on unix platforms - this is a terminator in C-based filesystem APIs. Slash (`/`) is also used as a path separator.
- Windows has a number of [reserved characters and names](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa365247(v=vs.85).aspx)(like`CON`,`PRN`, and`AUX`) which cannot legally be part of a filesystem component.
- Windows paths are [case-insensitive by default](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/case-sensitivity). So,`Foo.txt`and`foo.txt`are the same files on windows. But they are considered different paths on most unix systems.

A relative path that *accidentally* contains a platform-specific components
will largely result in a nonsensical paths being generated in the hope that
they will fail fast during development and testing.

```
use ;
use Path;
if cfg!
if cfg!
assert_eq!;
```

let relative_path = RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar");
let full_path = relative_path.to_path(&root);
assert_eq!(full_path, root.join("..\\foo\\.\\bar"));
// to_logical_path tries to apply the logical operations that the relative
// path corresponds to:
let relative_path = RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar");
let full_path = relative_path.to_logical_path(&root);
// Replicate the operation performed by `to_logical_path`.
let mut parent = root.clone();
parent.pop();
assert_eq!(full_path, parent.join("foo\\bar"));
```
When two relative paths are compared to each other, their exact component makeup determines equality.

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
assert_ne!(
    RelativePath::new("foo/bar/../baz"),
    RelativePath::new("foo/baz")
);
```
Using platform-specific path separators to construct relative paths is not supported.

Path separators from other platforms are simply treated as part of a component:

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
assert_ne!(
    RelativePath::new("foo/bar"),
    RelativePath::new("foo\\bar")
);
assert_eq!(1, RelativePath::new("foo\\bar").components().count());
assert_eq!(2, RelativePath::new("foo/bar").components().count());
```
To see if two relative paths are equivalent you can use [ normalize](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.normalize):

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
assert_eq!(
    RelativePath::new("foo/bar/../baz").normalize(),
    RelativePath::new("foo/baz").normalize(),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#additional-portability-notes)Additional portability notes

While relative paths avoid the most egregious portability issue, that absolute paths will work equally unwell on all platforms. We cannot avoid all. This section tries to document additional portability hazards that we are aware of.

[ RelativePath](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html), similarly to

[, makes no guarantees that its constituent components make up legal file names. While components are strictly separated by slashes, we can still store things in them which may not be used as legal paths on all platforms.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`- A `NUL`character is not permitted on unix platforms - this is a terminator in C-based filesystem APIs. Slash (`/`) is also used as a path separator.
- Windows has a number of [reserved characters and names](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa365247(v=vs.85).aspx)(like`CON`,`PRN`, and`AUX`) which cannot legally be part of a filesystem component.
- Windows paths are [case-insensitive by default](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/case-sensitivity). So,`Foo.txt`and`foo.txt`are the same files on windows. But they are considered different paths on most unix systems.

A relative path that *accidentally* contains a platform-specific components
will largely result in a nonsensical paths being generated in the hope that
they will fail fast during development and testing.

```
use relative_path::{RelativePath, PathExt};
use std::path::Path;
if cfg!(windows) {
    assert_eq!(
        Path::new("foo\\c:\\bar\\baz"),
        RelativePath::new("c:\\bar\\baz").to_path("foo")
    );
}
if cfg!(unix) {
    assert_eq!(
        Path::new("foo/bar/baz"),
        RelativePath::new("/bar/baz").to_path("foo")
    );
}
assert_eq!(
    Path::new("foo").relative_to("bar")?,
    RelativePath::new("../foo"),
);
```

# relative_path - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/relative-path/2.0.1/relative_path/index.html

## Expand description

Portable relative UTF-8 paths for Rust.

This crate provides a module analogous to [ std::path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/index.html), with the following
characteristics:

- The path separator is set to a fixed character (`/`), regardless of platform.
- Relative paths cannot represent a path in the filesystem without first
specifying *what they are relative to*using functions such as`to_path``to_logical_path`
- Relative paths are always guaranteed to be valid UTF-8 strings.

On top of this we support many operations that guarantee the same behavior across platforms.

For more utilities to manipulate relative paths, see the
[ relative-path-utils crate](https://docs.rs/relative-path-utils).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add `relative-path` to your `Cargo.toml`:

`relative-path = "2.0.1"`Start using relative paths:

```
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
use relative_path::RelativePath;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Manifest<'a> {
    #[serde(borrow)]
    source: &'a RelativePath,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serde-support)Serde Support

This library includes serde support that can be enabled with the `serde`
feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-is-stdpath-a-portability-hazard)Why is `std::path` a portability hazard?

Path representations differ across platforms.

- Windows permits using drive volumes (multiple roots) as a prefix (e.g.
`"c:\"`) and backslash (`\`) as a separator.
- Unix references absolute paths from a single root and uses forward slash
(`/`) as a separator.

If we use `PathBuf`, Storing paths in a manifest would allow our application
to build and run on one platform but potentially not others.

Consider the following data model and corresponding toml for a manifest:

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Manifest {
    source: PathBuf,
}
```
`source = "C:\\Users\\udoprog\\repo\\data\\source"`This will run for you (assuming `source` exists). So you go ahead and check
the manifest into git. The next day your Linux colleague calls you and
wonders what they have ever done to wrong you?

So what went wrong? Well two things. You forgot to make the `source`
relative, so anyone at the company which has a different username than you
won’t be able to use it. So you go ahead and fix that:

`source = "data\\source"`But there is still one problem! A backslash (`\`) is only a legal path
separator on Windows. Luckily you learn that forward slashes are supported
both on Windows *and* Linux. So you opt for:

`source = "data/source"`Things are working now. So all is well… Right? Sure, but we can do better.

This crate provides types that work with *portable relative paths* (hence
the name). So by using [ RelativePath](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html) we can systematically help avoid
portability issues like the one above. Avoiding issues at the source is
preferably over spending 5 minutes of onboarding time on a theoretical
problem, hoping that your new hires will remember what to do if they ever
encounter it.

Using [ RelativePathBuf](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePathBuf.html) we can fix our data model like this:

```
use relative_path::RelativePathBuf;
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Manifest {
    source: RelativePathBuf,
}
```
And where it’s used:

```
use std::fs;
use std::env::current_dir;
let manifest: Manifest = todo!();
let root = current_dir()?;
let source = manifest.source.to_path(&root);
let content = fs::read(&source)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Conversion to a platform-specific [ Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html) happens through the

[and](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.to_path)

`to_path`[functions. Where you are required to specify the path that prefixes the relative path. This can come from a function such as](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.to_logical_path)

`to_logical_path`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/env/fn.current_dir.html)

`std::env::current_dir````
use std::env::current_dir;
use std::path::Path;
use relative_path::RelativePath;
let root = current_dir()?;
// to_path unconditionally concatenates a relative path with its base:
let relative_path = RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar");
let full_path = relative_path.to_path(&root);
assert_eq!(full_path, root.join("..\\foo\\.\\bar"));
// to_logical_path tries to apply the logical operations that the relative
// path corresponds to:
let relative_path = RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar");
let full_path = relative_path.to_logical_path(&root);
// Replicate the operation performed by `to_logical_path`.
let mut parent = root.clone();
parent.pop();
assert_eq!(full_path, parent.join("foo\\bar"));
```
When two relative paths are compared to each other, their exact component makeup determines equality.

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
assert_ne!(
    RelativePath::new("foo/bar/../baz"),
    RelativePath::new("foo/baz")
);
```
Using platform-specific path separators to construct relative paths is not supported.

Path separators from other platforms are simply treated as part of a component:

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
assert_ne!(
    RelativePath::new("foo/bar"),
    RelativePath::new("foo\\bar")
);
assert_eq!(1, RelativePath::new("foo\\bar").components().count());
assert_eq!(2, RelativePath::new("foo/bar").components().count());
```
To see if two relative paths are equivalent you can use [ normalize](https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.normalize):

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
assert_eq!(
    RelativePath::new("foo/bar/../baz").normalize(),
    RelativePath::new("foo/baz").normalize(),
);
```

[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! let root = current_dir()?;
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! # if cfg!(windows) {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! // to_path unconditionally concatenates a relative path with its base:
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! let relative_path = RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar");
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! let full_path = relative_path.to_path(&root);
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! assert_eq!(full_path, root.join("..\\foo\\.\\bar"));
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! // to_logical_path tries to apply the logical operations that the relative
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! // path corresponds to:
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! let relative_path = RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar");
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! let full_path = relative_path.to_logical_path(&root);
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! // Replicate the operation performed by `to_logical_path`.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! let mut parent = root.clone();
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! parent.pop();
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! assert_eq!(full_path, parent.join("foo\\bar"));
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! # }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! # Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(())
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! ```
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! When two relative paths are compared to each other, their exact component
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! makeup determines equality.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! ```rust
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! use relative_path::RelativePath;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! assert_ne!(
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!     RelativePath::new("foo/bar/../baz"),
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!     RelativePath::new("foo/baz")
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! );
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! ```
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! Using platform-specific path separators to construct relative paths is not
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! supported.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! Path separators from other platforms are simply treated as part of a
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! component:
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! ```rust
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! use relative_path::RelativePath;
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! assert_ne!(
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!     RelativePath::new("foo/bar"),
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!     RelativePath::new("foo\\bar")
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! );
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! assert_eq!(1, RelativePath::new("foo\\bar").components().count());
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! assert_eq!(2, RelativePath::new("foo/bar").components().count());
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! ```
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! To see if two relative paths are equivalent you can use [`normalize`]:
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! ```rust
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! use relative_path::RelativePath;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! assert_eq!(
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!     RelativePath::new("foo/bar/../baz").normalize(),
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!     RelativePath::new("foo/baz").normalize(),
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! );
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! ```
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! <br>
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! ## Additional portability notes
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! While relative paths avoid the most egregious portability issue, that
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! absolute paths will work equally unwell on all platforms. We cannot avoid
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! all. This section tries to document additional portability hazards that we
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! are aware of.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! [`RelativePath`], similarly to [`Path`], makes no guarantees that its
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! constituent components make up legal file names. While components are
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! strictly separated by slashes, we can still store things in them which may
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! not be used as legal paths on all platforms.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! * A `NUL` character is not permitted on unix platforms - this is a
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!   terminator in C-based filesystem APIs. Slash (`/`) is also used as a path
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!   separator.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! * Windows has a number of [reserved characters and names][windows-reserved]
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!   (like `CON`, `PRN`, and `AUX`) which cannot legally be part of a
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!   filesystem component.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! * Windows paths are [case-insensitive by default][windows-case]. So,
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!   `Foo.txt` and `foo.txt` are the same files on windows. But they are
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!   considered different paths on most unix systems.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! A relative path that *accidentally* contains a platform-specific components
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! will largely result in a nonsensical paths being generated in the hope that
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! they will fail fast during development and testing.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! ```rust
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! use relative_path::{RelativePath, PathExt};
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! use std::path::Path;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! if cfg!(windows) {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!     assert_eq!(
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!         Path::new("foo\\c:\\bar\\baz"),
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!         RelativePath::new("c:\\bar\\baz").to_path("foo")
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!     );
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//! }
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//!
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! if cfg!(unix) {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!     assert_eq!(
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!         Path::new("foo/bar/baz"),
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!         RelativePath::new("/bar/baz").to_path("foo")
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!     );
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! assert_eq!(
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!     Path::new("foo").relative_to("bar")?,
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!     RelativePath::new("../foo"),
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! );
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! # Ok::<_, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! ```
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! [`None`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/enum.Option.html
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! [`normalize`]: https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html#method.normalize
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! [`Path`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! [`RelativePath`]: https://docs.rs/relative-path/1/relative_path/struct.RelativePath.html

[343](https://docs.rs#343)const STEM_SEP: char = '.';
[344](https://docs.rs#344)const CURRENT_STR: &str = ".";
[345](https://docs.rs#345)const PARENT_STR: &str = "..";
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)const SEP: char = '/';
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)#[inline(always)]
[350](https://docs.rs#350)fn split_file_at_dot(input: &str) -> (Option<&str>, Option<&str>) {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    if input == PARENT_STR {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        return (Some(input), None);
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    let mut iter = input.rsplitn(2, STEM_SEP);
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    let after = iter.next();
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    let before = iter.next();
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    if before == Some("") {
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        (Some(input), None)
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    } else {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        (before, after)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)}
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)// Iterate through `iter` while it matches `prefix`; return `None` if `prefix`
[368](https://docs.rs#368)// is not a prefix of `iter`, otherwise return `Some(iter_after_prefix)` giving
[369](https://docs.rs#369)// `iter` after having exhausted `prefix`.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)#[inline(always)]
[371](https://docs.rs#371)fn iter_after<'a, 'b, I, J>(mut iter: I, mut prefix: J) -> Option<I>
[372](https://docs.rs#372)where
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    I: Iterator<Item = Component<'a>> + Clone,
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    J: Iterator<Item = Component<'b>>,
[375](https://docs.rs#375){
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    loop {
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        let mut iter_next = iter.clone();
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        match (iter_next.next(), prefix.next()) {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            (Some(x), Some(y)) if x == y => (),
[380](https://docs.rs#380)            (Some(_) | None, Some(_)) => return None,
[381](https://docs.rs#381)            (Some(_) | None, None) => return Some(iter),
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        }
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        iter = iter_next;
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    }
[385](https://docs.rs#385)}

[387](https://docs.rs#387)/// A single path component.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)///
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// Accessed using the [`RelativePath::components`] iterator.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)///
[391](https://docs.rs#391)/// # Examples
[392](https://docs.rs#392)///
[393](https://docs.rs#393)/// ```
[394](https://docs.rs#394)/// use relative_path::{Component, RelativePath};
[395](https://docs.rs#395)///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)/// let path = RelativePath::new("foo/../bar/./baz");
[397](https://docs.rs#397)/// let mut it = path.components();
[398](https://docs.rs#398)///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)/// assert_eq!(Some(Component::Normal("foo")), it.next());
[400](https://docs.rs#400)/// assert_eq!(Some(Component::ParentDir), it.next());
[401](https://docs.rs#401)/// assert_eq!(Some(Component::Normal("bar")), it.next());
[402](https://docs.rs#402)/// assert_eq!(Some(Component::CurDir), it.next());
[403](https://docs.rs#403)/// assert_eq!(Some(Component::Normal("baz")), it.next());
[404](https://docs.rs#404)/// assert_eq!(None, it.next());
[405](https://docs.rs#405)/// ```
[406](https://docs.rs#406)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Hash, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
[407](https://docs.rs#407)pub enum Component<'a> {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// The current directory `.`.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    CurDir,
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// The parent directory `..`.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ParentDir,
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// A normal path component as a string.
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    Normal(&'a str),
[414](https://docs.rs#414)}
[415](https://docs.rs#415)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)impl<'a> Component<'a> {
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// Extracts the underlying [`str`] slice.
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// [`str`]: prim@str
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    ///
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// # Examples
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// ```
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// use relative_path::{RelativePath, Component};
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// let path = RelativePath::new("./tmp/../foo/bar.txt");
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    /// let components: Vec<_> = path.components().map(Component::as_str).collect();
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// assert_eq!(&components, &[".", "tmp", "..", "foo", "bar.txt"]);
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// ```
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    #[must_use]
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    #[inline]
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    pub fn as_str(self) -> &'a str {
[433](https://docs.rs#433)        use self::Component::{CurDir, Normal, ParentDir};
[434](https://docs.rs#434)
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        match self {
[436](https://docs.rs#436)            CurDir => CURRENT_STR,
[437](https://docs.rs#437)            ParentDir => PARENT_STR,
[438](https://docs.rs#438)            Normal(name) => name,
[439](https://docs.rs#439)        }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    }
[441](https://docs.rs#441)}

[473](https://docs.rs#473)/// Iterator over all the components in a relative path.
[474](https://docs.rs#474)#[derive(Clone)]
[475](https://docs.rs#475)pub struct Components<'a> {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    source: &'a str,
[477](https://docs.rs#477)}
[478](https://docs.rs#478)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)impl<'a> Iterator for Components<'a> {
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    type Item = Component<'a>;
[481](https://docs.rs#481)
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
[483](https://docs.rs#483)        self.source = self.source.trim_start_matches(SEP);
[484](https://docs.rs#484)
[485](https://docs.rs#485)        let slice = match self.source.find(SEP) {
[486](https://docs.rs#486)            Some(i) => {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)                let (slice, rest) = self.source.split_at(i);
[488](https://docs.rs#488)                self.source = rest.trim_start_matches(SEP);
[489](https://docs.rs#489)                slice
[490](https://docs.rs#490)            }
[491](https://docs.rs#491)            None => mem::take(&mut self.source),
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        };
[493](https://docs.rs#493)
[494](https://docs.rs#494)        match slice {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)            "" => None,
[496](https://docs.rs#496)            CURRENT_STR => Some(Component::CurDir),
[497](https://docs.rs#497)            PARENT_STR => Some(Component::ParentDir),
[498](https://docs.rs#498)            slice => Some(Component::Normal(slice)),
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        }
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    }
[501](https://docs.rs#501)}
[502](https://docs.rs#502)
[503](https://docs.rs#503)impl DoubleEndedIterator for Components<'_> {
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    fn next_back(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
[505](https://docs.rs#505)        self.source = self.source.trim_end_matches(SEP);
[506](https://docs.rs#506)
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        let slice = match self.source.rfind(SEP) {
[508](https://docs.rs#508)            Some(i) => {
[509](https://docs.rs#509)                let (rest, slice) = self.source.split_at(i + 1);
[510](https://docs.rs#510)                self.source = rest.trim_end_matches(SEP);
[511](https://docs.rs#511)                slice
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            }
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            None => mem::take(&mut self.source),
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        };
[515](https://docs.rs#515)
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        match slice {
[517](https://docs.rs#517)            "" => None,
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            CURRENT_STR => Some(Component::CurDir),
[519](https://docs.rs#519)            PARENT_STR => Some(Component::ParentDir),
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            slice => Some(Component::Normal(slice)),
[521](https://docs.rs#521)        }
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    }
[523](https://docs.rs#523)}
[524](https://docs.rs#524)
[525](https://docs.rs#525)impl<'a> Components<'a> {
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    /// Construct a new component from the given string.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    #[inline]
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    fn new(source: &'a str) -> Components<'a> {
[529](https://docs.rs#529)        Self { source }
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    }
[531](https://docs.rs#531)
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    /// Extracts a slice corresponding to the portion of the path remaining for iteration.

[681](https://docs.rs#681)
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    /// Try to convert a [`Path`] to a [`RelativePath`] without allocating a buffer.
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    ///
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    /// [`Path`]: std::path::Path
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    ///
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// # Errors
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    ///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// This requires the path to be a legal, platform-neutral relative path.
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// Otherwise various forms of [`FromPathError`] will be returned as an
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// [`Err`].
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    ///
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    /// # Examples
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    ///
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    /// ```
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// use relative_path::{RelativePath, FromPathErrorKind};
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    ///
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// assert_eq!(
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    ///     Ok(RelativePath::new("foo/bar")),
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    ///     RelativePath::from_path("foo/bar")
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    /// );
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    ///
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// // Note: absolute paths are different depending on platform.
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    /// if cfg!(windows) {
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    ///     let e = RelativePath::from_path("c:\\foo\\bar").unwrap_err();
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    ///     assert_eq!(FromPathErrorKind::NonRelative, e.kind());
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// }
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    ///
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    /// if cfg!(unix) {
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    ///     let e = RelativePath::from_path("/foo/bar").unwrap_err();
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    ///     assert_eq!(FromPathErrorKind::NonRelative, e.kind());
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    /// }
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    /// ```
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    #[cfg(feature = "std")]
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    #[cfg_attr(relative_path_docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "std")))]
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    pub fn from_path<P>(path: &P) -> Result<&RelativePath, FromPathError>
[716](https://docs.rs#716)    where
[717](https://docs.rs#717)        P: ?Sized + AsRef<path::Path>,
[718](https://docs.rs#718)    {
[719](https://docs.rs#719)        use std::path::Component::{CurDir, Normal, ParentDir, Prefix, RootDir};
[720](https://docs.rs#720)
[721](https://docs.rs#721)        let other = path.as_ref();
[722](https://docs.rs#722)
[723](https://docs.rs#723)        let s = match other.to_str() {
[724](https://docs.rs#724)            Some(s) => s,
[725](https://docs.rs#725)            None => return Err(FromPathErrorKind::NonUtf8.into()),
[726](https://docs.rs#726)        };
[727](https://docs.rs#727)
[728](https://docs.rs#728)        let rel = RelativePath::new(s);
[729](https://docs.rs#729)
[730](https://docs.rs#730)        // check that the component compositions are equal.
[731](https://docs.rs#731)        for (a, b) in other.components().zip(rel.components()) {
[732](https://docs.rs#732)            match (a, b) {
[733](https://docs.rs#733)                (Prefix(_) | RootDir, _) => return Err(FromPathErrorKind::NonRelative.into()),
[734](https://docs.rs#734)                (CurDir, Component::CurDir) | (ParentDir, Component::ParentDir) => continue,
[735](https://docs.rs#735)                (Normal(a), Component::Normal(b)) if a == b => continue,
[736](https://docs.rs#736)                _ => return Err(FromPathErrorKind::BadSeparator.into()),
[737](https://docs.rs#737)            }
[738](https://docs.rs#738)        }
[739](https://docs.rs#739)
[740](https://docs.rs#740)        Ok(rel)
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    }
[742](https://docs.rs#742)
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// Yields the underlying [`str`] slice.
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    ///
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    /// [`str`]: prim@str
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    ///
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    /// # Examples
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    ///
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    /// ```
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;

[856](https://docs.rs#856)    /// Build an owned [`PathBuf`] relative to `base` for the current relative
[857](https://docs.rs#857)    /// path.
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    ///
[859](https://docs.rs#859)    /// # Examples
[860](https://docs.rs#860)    ///
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    /// ```
[862](https://docs.rs#862)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    /// use std::path::Path;
[864](https://docs.rs#864)    ///
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    /// let path = RelativePath::new("foo/bar").to_path(".");
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    /// assert_eq!(Path::new("./foo/bar"), path);
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    ///
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    /// let path = RelativePath::new("foo/bar").to_path("");
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    /// assert_eq!(Path::new("foo/bar"), path);
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    /// ```
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    ///
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    /// # Encoding an absolute path
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    ///
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    /// Absolute paths are, in contrast to when using [`PathBuf::push`] *ignored*
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    /// and will be added unchanged to the buffer.
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    ///
[877](https://docs.rs#877)    /// This is to preserve the probability of a path conversion failing if the
[878](https://docs.rs#878)    /// relative path contains platform-specific absolute path components.
[879](https://docs.rs#879)    ///
[880](https://docs.rs#880)    /// ```
[881](https://docs.rs#881)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[882](https://docs.rs#882)    /// use std::path::Path;
[883](https://docs.rs#883)    ///
[884](https://docs.rs#884)    /// if cfg!(windows) {
[885](https://docs.rs#885)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("/bar/baz").to_path("foo");
[886](https://docs.rs#886)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo\\bar\\baz"), path);
[887](https://docs.rs#887)    ///
[888](https://docs.rs#888)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("c:\\bar\\baz").to_path("foo");
[889](https://docs.rs#889)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo\\c:\\bar\\baz"), path);
[890](https://docs.rs#890)    /// }
[891](https://docs.rs#891)    ///
[892](https://docs.rs#892)    /// if cfg!(unix) {
[893](https://docs.rs#893)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("/bar/baz").to_path("foo");
[894](https://docs.rs#894)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo/bar/baz"), path);
[895](https://docs.rs#895)    ///
[896](https://docs.rs#896)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("c:\\bar\\baz").to_path("foo");
[897](https://docs.rs#897)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo/c:\\bar\\baz"), path);
[898](https://docs.rs#898)    /// }
[899](https://docs.rs#899)    /// ```
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    ///
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    /// [`PathBuf`]: std::path::PathBuf
[902](https://docs.rs#902)    /// [`PathBuf::push`]: std::path::PathBuf::push
[903](https://docs.rs#903)    #[cfg(feature = "std")]
[904](https://docs.rs#904)    #[cfg_attr(relative_path_docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "std")))]
[905](https://docs.rs#905)    #[must_use]
[906](https://docs.rs#906)    pub fn to_path<P>(&self, base: P) -> path::PathBuf
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    where
[908](https://docs.rs#908)        P: AsRef<path::Path>,
[909](https://docs.rs#909)    {
[910](https://docs.rs#910)        let mut p = base.as_ref().to_path_buf().into_os_string();
[911](https://docs.rs#911)
[912](https://docs.rs#912)        for c in self.components() {
[913](https://docs.rs#913)            if !p.is_empty() {
[914](https://docs.rs#914)                p.push(path::MAIN_SEPARATOR.encode_utf8(&mut [0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8]));
[915](https://docs.rs#915)            }
[916](https://docs.rs#916)
[917](https://docs.rs#917)            p.push(c.as_str());
[918](https://docs.rs#918)        }
[919](https://docs.rs#919)
[920](https://docs.rs#920)        path::PathBuf::from(p)
[921](https://docs.rs#921)    }
[922](https://docs.rs#922)
[923](https://docs.rs#923)    /// Build an owned [`PathBuf`] relative to `base` for the current relative
[924](https://docs.rs#924)    /// path.
[925](https://docs.rs#925)    ///
[926](https://docs.rs#926)    /// This is similar to [`to_path`] except that it doesn't just
[927](https://docs.rs#927)    /// unconditionally append one path to the other, instead it performs the
[928](https://docs.rs#928)    /// following operations depending on its own components:
[929](https://docs.rs#929)    ///
[930](https://docs.rs#930)    /// * [`Component::CurDir`] leaves the `base` unmodified.
[931](https://docs.rs#931)    /// * [`Component::ParentDir`] removes a component from `base` using
[932](https://docs.rs#932)    ///   [`path::PathBuf::pop`].
[933](https://docs.rs#933)    /// * [`Component::Normal`] pushes the given path component onto `base`
[934](https://docs.rs#934)    ///   using the same mechanism as [`to_path`].
[935](https://docs.rs#935)    ///
[936](https://docs.rs#936)    /// [`to_path`]: RelativePath::to_path
[937](https://docs.rs#937)    ///
[938](https://docs.rs#938)    /// Note that the exact semantics of the path operation is determined by the
[939](https://docs.rs#939)    /// corresponding [`PathBuf`] operation. E.g. popping a component off a path
[940](https://docs.rs#940)    /// like `.` will result in an empty path.
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    ///
[942](https://docs.rs#942)    /// ```
[943](https://docs.rs#943)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[944](https://docs.rs#944)    /// use std::path::Path;
[945](https://docs.rs#945)    ///
[946](https://docs.rs#946)    /// let path = RelativePath::new("..").to_logical_path(".");
[947](https://docs.rs#947)    /// assert_eq!(path, Path::new(""));
[948](https://docs.rs#948)    /// ```
[949](https://docs.rs#949)    ///
[950](https://docs.rs#950)    /// # Examples
[951](https://docs.rs#951)    ///
[952](https://docs.rs#952)    /// ```
[953](https://docs.rs#953)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[954](https://docs.rs#954)    /// use std::path::Path;
[955](https://docs.rs#955)    ///
[956](https://docs.rs#956)    /// let path = RelativePath::new("..").to_logical_path("foo/bar");
[957](https://docs.rs#957)    /// assert_eq!(path, Path::new("foo"));
[958](https://docs.rs#958)    /// ```
[959](https://docs.rs#959)    ///
[960](https://docs.rs#960)    /// # Encoding an absolute path
[961](https://docs.rs#961)    ///
[962](https://docs.rs#962)    /// Behaves the same as [`to_path`][RelativePath::to_path] when encoding
[963](https://docs.rs#963)    /// absolute paths.
[964](https://docs.rs#964)    ///
[965](https://docs.rs#965)    /// Absolute paths are, in contrast to when using [`PathBuf::push`] *ignored*
[966](https://docs.rs#966)    /// and will be added unchanged to the buffer.
[967](https://docs.rs#967)    ///
[968](https://docs.rs#968)    /// This is to preserve the probability of a path conversion failing if the
[969](https://docs.rs#969)    /// relative path contains platform-specific absolute path components.
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    ///
[971](https://docs.rs#971)    /// ```
[972](https://docs.rs#972)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    /// use std::path::Path;
[974](https://docs.rs#974)    ///
[975](https://docs.rs#975)    /// if cfg!(windows) {
[976](https://docs.rs#976)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("/bar/baz").to_logical_path("foo");
[977](https://docs.rs#977)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo\\bar\\baz"), path);
[978](https://docs.rs#978)    ///
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("c:\\bar\\baz").to_logical_path("foo");
[980](https://docs.rs#980)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo\\c:\\bar\\baz"), path);
[981](https://docs.rs#981)    ///
[982](https://docs.rs#982)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("foo/bar").to_logical_path("");
[983](https://docs.rs#983)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo\\bar"), path);
[984](https://docs.rs#984)    /// }
[985](https://docs.rs#985)    ///
[986](https://docs.rs#986)    /// if cfg!(unix) {
[987](https://docs.rs#987)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("/bar/baz").to_logical_path("foo");
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo/bar/baz"), path);
[989](https://docs.rs#989)    ///
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("c:\\bar\\baz").to_logical_path("foo");
[991](https://docs.rs#991)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo/c:\\bar\\baz"), path);
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    ///
[993](https://docs.rs#993)    ///     let path = RelativePath::new("foo/bar").to_logical_path("");
[994](https://docs.rs#994)    ///     assert_eq!(Path::new("foo/bar"), path);
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    /// }
[996](https://docs.rs#996)    /// ```
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    ///
[998](https://docs.rs#998)    /// [`PathBuf`]: std::path::PathBuf
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    /// [`PathBuf::push`]: std::path::PathBuf::push
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    #[cfg(feature = "std")]
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    #[cfg_attr(relative_path_docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "std")))]
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    #[must_use]
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    pub fn to_logical_path<P>(&self, base: P) -> path::PathBuf
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    where
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)        P: AsRef<path::Path>,
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)    {
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)        use self::Component::{CurDir, Normal, ParentDir};
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)        let mut p = base.as_ref().to_path_buf().into_os_string();
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)        for c in self.components() {
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)            match c {
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)                CurDir => continue,
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)                ParentDir => {
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)                    let mut temp = path::PathBuf::from(std::mem::take(&mut p));
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)                    temp.pop();
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)                    p = temp.into_os_string();
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)                }
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)                Normal(c) => {
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)                    if !p.is_empty() {
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)                        p.push(path::MAIN_SEPARATOR.encode_utf8(&mut [0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8]));
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)                    }
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)                    p.push(c);
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)                }
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)            }
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)        }
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)        path::PathBuf::from(p)
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    }
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)    /// Returns a relative path, without its final [`Component`] if there is one.
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)    ///
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)    /// # Examples
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)    ///
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)    /// ```
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)    ///
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)    /// assert_eq!(Some(RelativePath::new("foo")), RelativePath::new("foo/bar").parent());
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)    /// assert_eq!(Some(RelativePath::new("")), RelativePath::new("foo").parent());
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)    /// assert_eq!(None, RelativePath::new("").parent());
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)    /// ```
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)    #[must_use]
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)    pub fn parent(&self) -> Option<&RelativePath> {
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)        use self::Component::CurDir;
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)        if self.inner.is_empty() {
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)            return None;
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)        }
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)        let mut it = self.components();
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)        while let Some(CurDir) = it.next_back() {}
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)        Some(it.as_relative_path())
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)    }
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)    /// Returns the final component of the `RelativePath`, if there is one.
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)    ///
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)    /// If the path is a normal file, this is the file name. If it's the path of
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)    /// a directory, this is the directory name.
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)    ///
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)    /// Returns [`None`] If the path terminates in `..`.
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)    ///
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)    /// # Examples
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)    ///
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)    /// ```
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)    ///
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)    /// assert_eq!(Some("bin"), RelativePath::new("usr/bin/").file_name());
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)    /// assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), RelativePath::new("tmp/foo.txt").file_name());
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)    /// assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), RelativePath::new("tmp/foo.txt/").file_name());
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)    /// assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), RelativePath::new("foo.txt/.").file_name());
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)    /// assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), RelativePath::new("foo.txt/.//").file_name());
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)    /// assert_eq!(None, RelativePath::new("foo.txt/..").file_name());
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)    /// assert_eq!(None, RelativePath::new("/").file_name());
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)    /// ```
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)    #[must_use]
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)    pub fn file_name(&self) -> Option<&str> {
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)        use self::Component::{CurDir, Normal, ParentDir};
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)        let mut it = self.components();
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)        while let Some(c) = it.next_back() {
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)            return match c {
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)                CurDir => continue,
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)                Normal(name) => Some(name),
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)                ParentDir => None,
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)            };
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)        }
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)        None
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)    }

[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)    /// Determines whether `self` is normalized.

[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)    /// # Examples

[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)    /// assert!(RelativePath::new("foo/bar/baz.txt").is_normalized());
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)    /// assert!(RelativePath::new("..").is_normalized());
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)    /// assert!(RelativePath::new("../..").is_normalized());
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)    /// assert!(RelativePath::new("../../foo/bar/baz.txt").is_normalized());
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)    ///
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)    /// // These are not normalized.
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new(".").is_normalized());
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new("./baz.txt").is_normalized());
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new("foo/..").is_normalized());
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new("foo/../baz.txt").is_normalized());
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new("foo/.").is_normalized());
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new("foo/./baz.txt").is_normalized());
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)    /// assert!(!RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar/../baz.txt").is_normalized());
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)    /// ```
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)    #[must_use]
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)    pub fn is_normalized(&self) -> bool {
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)        self.components()
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)            .skip_while(|c| matches!(c, Component::ParentDir))
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)            .all(|c| matches!(c, Component::Normal(_)))
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)    }

[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)    /// Extracts the stem (non-extension) portion of [`file_name`][Self::file_name].
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    ///
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)    /// The stem is:
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)    ///
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)    /// * [`None`], if there is no file name;
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)    /// * The entire file name if there is no embedded `.`;
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)    /// * The entire file name if the file name begins with `.` and has no other `.`s within;
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)    /// * Otherwise, the portion of the file name before the final `.`
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)    ///
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)    /// # Examples
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)    ///
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)    /// ```
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)    ///
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)    /// let path = RelativePath::new("foo.rs");
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)    ///
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)    /// assert_eq!("foo", path.file_stem().unwrap());
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)    /// ```
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    #[must_use]

[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)    /// Extracts the extension of [`file_name`][Self::file_name], if possible.
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    ///
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)    /// The extension is:
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    ///
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)    /// * [`None`], if there is no file name;
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    /// * [`None`], if there is no embedded `.`;
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    /// * [`None`], if the file name begins with `.` and has no other `.`s within;
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)    /// * Otherwise, the portion of the file name after the final `.`
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)    ///
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)    /// # Examples
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)    ///
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)    /// ```
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)    ///
[1266](https://docs.rs#1266)    /// assert_eq!(Some("rs"), RelativePath::new("foo.rs").extension());
[1267](https://docs.rs#1267)    /// assert_eq!(None, RelativePath::new(".rs").extension());
[1268](https://docs.rs#1268)    /// assert_eq!(Some("rs"), RelativePath::new("foo.rs/.").extension());
[1269](https://docs.rs#1269)    /// ```
[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)    #[must_use]
[1271](https://docs.rs#1271)    pub fn extension(&self) -> Option<&str> {
[1272](https://docs.rs#1272)        self.file_name()
[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)            .map(split_file_at_dot)
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)            .and_then(|(before, after)| before.and(after))
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)    }

[1335](https://docs.rs#1335)    /// Return an owned [`RelativePathBuf`], with all non-normal components
[1336](https://docs.rs#1336)    /// moved to the beginning of the path.
[1337](https://docs.rs#1337)    ///
[1338](https://docs.rs#1338)    /// This permits for a normalized representation of different relative
[1339](https://docs.rs#1339)    /// components.
[1340](https://docs.rs#1340)    ///
[1341](https://docs.rs#1341)    /// Normalization is a _destructive_ operation if the path references an
[1342](https://docs.rs#1342)    /// actual filesystem path. An example of this is symlinks under unix, a
[1343](https://docs.rs#1343)    /// path like `foo/../bar` might reference a different location other than
[1344](https://docs.rs#1344)    /// `./bar`.
[1345](https://docs.rs#1345)    ///
[1346](https://docs.rs#1346)    /// Normalization is a logical operation and does not guarantee that the
[1347](https://docs.rs#1347)    /// constructed path corresponds to what the filesystem would do. On Linux
[1348](https://docs.rs#1348)    /// for example symbolic links could mean that the logical path doesn't
[1349](https://docs.rs#1349)    /// correspond to the filesystem path.
[1350](https://docs.rs#1350)    ///
[1351](https://docs.rs#1351)    /// # Examples
[1352](https://docs.rs#1352)    ///
[1353](https://docs.rs#1353)    /// ```
[1354](https://docs.rs#1354)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1355](https://docs.rs#1355)    ///
[1356](https://docs.rs#1356)    /// assert_eq!(
[1357](https://docs.rs#1357)    ///     "../foo/baz.txt",
[1358](https://docs.rs#1358)    ///     RelativePath::new("../foo/./bar/../baz.txt").normalize()
[1359](https://docs.rs#1359)    /// );
[1360](https://docs.rs#1360)    ///
[1361](https://docs.rs#1361)    /// assert_eq!(
[1362](https://docs.rs#1362)    ///     "",
[1363](https://docs.rs#1363)    ///     RelativePath::new(".").normalize()
[1364](https://docs.rs#1364)    /// );
[1365](https://docs.rs#1365)    /// ```
[1366](https://docs.rs#1366)    #[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[1367](https://docs.rs#1367)    #[cfg_attr(relative_path_docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "alloc")))]
[1368](https://docs.rs#1368)    #[must_use]
[1369](https://docs.rs#1369)    pub fn normalize(&self) -> RelativePathBuf {
[1370](https://docs.rs#1370)        let mut buf = RelativePathBuf::with_capacity(self.inner.len());
[1371](https://docs.rs#1371)        self::relative_path_buf::relative_traversal(&mut buf, self.components());
[1372](https://docs.rs#1372)        buf
[1373](https://docs.rs#1373)    }
[1374](https://docs.rs#1374)
[1375](https://docs.rs#1375)    /// Constructs a relative path from the current path, to `path`.
[1376](https://docs.rs#1376)    ///
[1377](https://docs.rs#1377)    /// This function will return the empty [`RelativePath`] `""` if this source
[1378](https://docs.rs#1378)    /// contains unnamed components like `..` that would have to be traversed to
[1379](https://docs.rs#1379)    /// reach the destination `path`. This is necessary since we have no way of
[1380](https://docs.rs#1380)    /// knowing what the names of those components are when we're building the
[1381](https://docs.rs#1381)    /// new relative path.
[1382](https://docs.rs#1382)    ///
[1383](https://docs.rs#1383)    /// ```
[1384](https://docs.rs#1384)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1385](https://docs.rs#1385)    ///
[1386](https://docs.rs#1386)    /// // Here we don't know what directories `../..` refers to, so there's no
[1387](https://docs.rs#1387)    /// // way to construct a path back to `bar` in the current directory from
[1388](https://docs.rs#1388)    /// // `../..`.
[1389](https://docs.rs#1389)    /// let from = RelativePath::new("../../foo/relative-path");
[1390](https://docs.rs#1390)    /// let to = RelativePath::new("bar");
[1391](https://docs.rs#1391)    /// assert_eq!("", from.relative(to));
[1392](https://docs.rs#1392)    /// ```
[1393](https://docs.rs#1393)    ///
[1394](https://docs.rs#1394)    /// One exception to this is when two paths contains a common prefix at
[1395](https://docs.rs#1395)    /// which point there's no need to know what the names of those unnamed
[1396](https://docs.rs#1396)    /// components are.
[1397](https://docs.rs#1397)    ///
[1398](https://docs.rs#1398)    /// ```
[1399](https://docs.rs#1399)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1400](https://docs.rs#1400)    ///
[1401](https://docs.rs#1401)    /// let from = RelativePath::new("../../foo/bar");
[1402](https://docs.rs#1402)    /// let to = RelativePath::new("../../foo/baz");
[1403](https://docs.rs#1403)    ///
[1404](https://docs.rs#1404)    /// assert_eq!("../baz", from.relative(to));
[1405](https://docs.rs#1405)    ///
[1406](https://docs.rs#1406)    /// let from = RelativePath::new("../a/../../foo/bar");
[1407](https://docs.rs#1407)    /// let to = RelativePath::new("../../foo/baz");
[1408](https://docs.rs#1408)    ///
[1409](https://docs.rs#1409)    /// assert_eq!("../baz", from.relative(to));
[1410](https://docs.rs#1410)    /// ```
[1411](https://docs.rs#1411)    ///
[1412](https://docs.rs#1412)    /// # Examples
[1413](https://docs.rs#1413)    ///
[1414](https://docs.rs#1414)    /// ```
[1415](https://docs.rs#1415)    /// use relative_path::RelativePath;
[1416](https://docs.rs#1416)    ///
[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)    /// assert_eq!(
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)    ///     "../../e/f",
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)    ///     RelativePath::new("a/b/c/d").relative(RelativePath::new("a/b/e/f"))
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)    /// );
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)    ///
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)    /// assert_eq!(
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)    ///     "../bbb",
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)    ///     RelativePath::new("a/../aaa").relative(RelativePath::new("b/../bbb"))
[1425](https://docs.rs#1425)    /// );
[1426](https://docs.rs#1426)    ///
[1427](https://docs.rs#1427)    /// let a = RelativePath::new("git/relative-path");
[1428](https://docs.rs#1428)    /// let b = RelativePath::new("git");
[1429](https://docs.rs#1429)    /// assert_eq!("relative-path", b.relative(a));
[1430](https://docs.rs#1430)    /// assert_eq!("..", a.relative(b));
[1431](https://docs.rs#1431)    ///
[1432](https://docs.rs#1432)    /// let a = RelativePath::new("foo/bar/bap/foo.h");
[1433](https://docs.rs#1433)    /// let b = RelativePath::new("../arch/foo.h");
[1434](https://docs.rs#1434)    /// assert_eq!("../../../../../arch/foo.h", a.relative(b));
[1435](https://docs.rs#1435)    /// assert_eq!("", b.relative(a));
[1436](https://docs.rs#1436)    /// ```
[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)    #[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)    #[cfg_attr(relative_path_docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "alloc")))]
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)    #[must_use]
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)    pub fn relative<P>(&self, path: P) -> RelativePathBuf
[1441](https://docs.rs#1441)    where
[1442](https://docs.rs#1442)        P: AsRef<RelativePath>,
[1443](https://docs.rs#1443)    {
[1444](https://docs.rs#1444)        let mut from = RelativePathBuf::with_capacity(self.inner.len());
[1445](https://docs.rs#1445)        let mut to = RelativePathBuf::with_capacity(path.as_ref().inner.len());
[1446](https://docs.rs#1446)
[1447](https://docs.rs#1447)        self::relative_path_buf::relative_traversal(&mut from, self.components());
[1448](https://docs.rs#1448)        self::relative_path_buf::relative_traversal(&mut to, path.as_ref().components());
[1449](https://docs.rs#1449)
[1450](https://docs.rs#1450)        let mut it_from = from.components();
[1451](https://docs.rs#1451)        let mut it_to = to.components();
[1452](https://docs.rs#1452)
[1453](https://docs.rs#1453)        // Strip a common prefixes - if any.
[1454](https://docs.rs#1454)        let (lead_from, lead_to) = loop {
[1455](https://docs.rs#1455)            match (it_from.next(), it_to.next()) {
[1456](https://docs.rs#1456)                (Some(f), Some(t)) if f == t => continue,
[1457](https://docs.rs#1457)                (f, t) => {
[1458](https://docs.rs#1458)                    break (f, t);
[1459](https://docs.rs#1459)                }
[1460](https://docs.rs#1460)            }
[1461](https://docs.rs#1461)        };
[1462](https://docs.rs#1462)
[1463](https://docs.rs#1463)        // Special case: The path we are traversing from can't contain unnamed
[1464](https://docs.rs#1464)        // components. A relative path might be any path, like `/`, or
[1465](https://docs.rs#1465)        // `/foo/bar/baz`, and these components cannot be named in the relative
[1466](https://docs.rs#1466)        // traversal.
[1467](https://docs.rs#1467)        //
[1468](https://docs.rs#1468)        // Also note that `relative_traversal` guarantees that all ParentDir
[1469](https://docs.rs#1469)        // components are at the head of the path being built.
[1470](https://docs.rs#1470)        if lead_from == Some(Component::ParentDir) {
[1471](https://docs.rs#1471)            return RelativePathBuf::new();
[1472](https://docs.rs#1472)        }
[1473](https://docs.rs#1473)
[1474](https://docs.rs#1474)        let head = lead_from.into_iter().chain(it_from);
[1475](https://docs.rs#1475)        let tail = lead_to.into_iter().chain(it_to);
[1476](https://docs.rs#1476)
[1477](https://docs.rs#1477)        let mut buf = RelativePathBuf::with_capacity(usize::max(from.len(), to.len()));
[1478](https://docs.rs#1478)
[1479](https://docs.rs#1479)        for c in head.map(|_| Component::ParentDir).chain(tail) {
[1480](https://docs.rs#1480)            buf.push(c.as_str());
[1481](https://docs.rs#1481)        }
[1482](https://docs.rs#1482)
[1483](https://docs.rs#1483)        buf
[1484](https://docs.rs#1484)    }
[1485](https://docs.rs#1485)
[1486](https://docs.rs#1486)    /// Check if path starts with a path separator.
[1487](https://docs.rs#1487)    #[inline]
[1488](https://docs.rs#1488)    #[cfg(feature = "alloc")]

# Components in relative_path - Rust

`pub struct Components<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Iterator over all the components in a relative path.

#### pub fn [as_relative_path](https://docs.rs#method.as_relative_path)(&self) -> &'a [RelativePath](https://docs.rs/struct.RelativePath.html)

Extracts a slice corresponding to the portion of the path remaining for iteration.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use relative_path::RelativePath;
let mut components = RelativePath::new("tmp/foo/bar.txt").components();
components.next();
components.next();
assert_eq!("bar.txt", components.as_relative_path());
```

# Display in relative_path - Rust

`pub struct Display<'a> { /* private fields */ }`RelativePath implements std::fmt::Display directly

## Expand description

Helper struct for printing relative paths.

This is not strictly necessary in the same sense as it is for [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html),
because relative paths are guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. But the behavior is
preserved to simplify the transition between

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RelativePath.html)

An owned, mutable relative path.

This type provides methods to manipulate relative path objects.

**crate feature**only.

`std`Try to convert a [ Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html) to a

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RelativePathBuf.html)

`RelativePathBuf`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use relative_path::{RelativePath, RelativePathBuf, FromPathErrorKind};
use std::path::Path;
assert_eq!(
    Ok(RelativePath::new("foo/bar").to_owned()),
    RelativePathBuf::from_path(Path::new("foo/bar"))
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

This will error in case the provided path is not a relative path, which
is identifier by it having a [ Prefix](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/enum.Component.html#variant.Prefix) or

[component.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/enum.Component.html#variant.RootDir)

`RootDir`Extends `self` with `path`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use relative_path::RelativePathBuf;
let mut path = RelativePathBuf::new();
path.push("foo");
path.push("bar");
assert_eq!("foo/bar", path);
let mut path = RelativePathBuf::new();
path.push("foo");
path.push("/bar");
assert_eq!("foo/bar", path);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/relative_path/relative_path_buf.rs.html#197-207)#### pub fn [set_file_name](https://docs.rs#method.set_file_name)<S>(&mut self, file_name: S)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/relative_path/relative_path_buf.rs.html#197-207)

#### pub fn [set_file_name](https://docs.rs#method.set_file_name)<S>(&mut self, file_name: S)

Updates [ file_name](https://docs.rs/struct.RelativePath.html#method.file_name) to

`file_name`.If [ file_name](https://docs.rs/struct.RelativePath.html#method.file_name) was

[, this is equivalent to pushing](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/enum.Option.html)

`None``file_name`.Otherwise it is equivalent to calling [ pop](https://docs.rs/struct.RelativePathBuf.html#method.pop) and then pushing

`file_name`. The new path will be a sibling of the original path. (That
is, it will have the same parent.)[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use relative_path::RelativePathBuf;
let mut buf = RelativePathBuf::from("");
assert!(buf.file_name() == None);
buf.set_file_name("bar");
assert_eq!(RelativePathBuf::from("bar"), buf);
assert!(buf.file_name().is_some());
buf.set_file_name("baz.txt");
assert_eq!(RelativePathBuf::from("baz.txt"), buf);
buf.push("bar");
assert!(buf.file_name().is_some());
buf.set_file_name("bar.txt");
assert_eq!(RelativePathBuf::from("baz.txt/bar.txt"), buf);
```
